title: What the Ground Knows
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 6 of 40
content:
Toph decided I needed self-defense lessons because I lost an argument with a crate.

The crate had been falling from a loading platform.

The following morning Toph marched me back to the same loading platform. A worker was there inspecting a frayed rope, and the entire crate had been lowered onto the ground.

“See?” Toph said. “Not a mysterious attack by boxes. Somebody tied a bad knot.”

The worker looked defensive. “I didn't tie that one.”

“Didn't say you did. I'm saying we're fixing the problem before Paperwork here practices being crushed again.”

I wanted to be offended by the nickname. Instead I watched her find the loose end with her fingers, test the rope's tension, and call the foreman over to explain where the platform needed a second stop.

“You're not teaching me to fight crates,” I said.

“Congratulations. You're learning to notice when they're about to become somebody else's problem.”

The foreman promised to check the rest of the hoist. Toph asked him to put the result on the job board and tell the next shift, not just us. She wasn't asking for a medal; she wanted to know no one would stand beneath an unsafe load after we went home.

When we reached the yard she picked up a padded staff.

“Now,” she said, “about that self-defense lesson. I'm going to be right here. You can tell me to stop whenever you need.”

“Does that make the next half-hour less terrifying?”

“Nope.” She grinned. “But it makes it yours.”

I had been standing under it.

I moved in time, which I considered a victory.

Toph considered the entire incident a personal insult.

“You froze.”

“For half a second.”

“That’s enough time to get flattened.”

“I did not get flattened.”

“Because I was there.”

“You’re very humble.”

“I’m the greatest earthbender in the world. Humility would be lying.”

That was how I found myself barefoot in the courtyard behind her metalbending school at dawn, regretting every choice that had led me there.

“I’m not an earthbender,” I reminded her.

“No kidding.”

“I cannot feel the ground the way you do.”

“Also noticed.”

“What, exactly, are you teaching me?”

Toph planted one heel and folded her arms. “How to stop acting like being a nonbender means your only choices are run or wait for somebody shinier to save you.”

The words hit harder than the crate would have.

I stared at her.

Toph’s expression did not change.

“Too mean?” she asked.

“No.”

“Good.”

She tossed me a padded practice staff.

The first lesson was not fighting.

It was balance.

Toph made me stand with my knees bent while she shoved my shoulders from different angles. Every time I stumbled, she called me a decorative fence post. Every time I corrected, she said nothing—which I quickly learned was praise.

“Stop trying to guess where I’m going,” she said.

“I’d love to. You’re hitting me.”

“I’m barely touching you.”

“You throw rocks for fun. Your scale is broken.”

A grin flashed across her face.

She came at me again.

This time I did not try to outthink her. I felt the pressure through my feet, the change in my center, the direction of her hand. I stepped instead of locking my knees.

Toph’s palm slid past my shoulder.

“There.”

I blinked.

“That was good?”

“Don’t ruin it.”

We worked until sweat dampened my shirt and the city began waking beyond the school walls.

Toph moved through the courtyard as if every inch belonged to her because, in a way, it did. She knew where I stood from the tremor of my weight. She knew when a student entered the far gate. She knew when a cart rolled down the street outside.

She also knew when I watched her.

“Again,” she said.

“I need water.”

“You need to stop staring at my arms.”

I nearly dropped the staff.

Toph laughed so hard she had to brace a hand on her knee.

“I was not—”

“Your heartbeat did the thing.”

“My heartbeat is none of your business.”

“It’s stomping on my business.”

I threw the padded staff at her.

She caught it.

Of course she did.

“Violence,” she said approvingly. “We’re making progress.”

I sat on the courtyard step and drank from my flask.

Toph dropped down beside me.

For a few minutes, we listened to the sounds of the school. Metal doors. Student voices. Someone swearing after apparently bending the wrong piece of railing.

“You built this fast,” I said.

“People wanted to learn.”

“That isn’t what I meant.”

Toph tilted her head.

I looked across the courtyard. “You made a place where nobody gets told their way of sensing the world is wrong.”

Her face went still.

I immediately worried I had stepped somewhere private.

Then she picked at a chip in the stone beside her foot.

“My parents had rooms for everything,” she said. “Music. Tea. Guests. Lessons. Rooms nobody used because they were supposed to look nice.”

I waited.

“They didn’t have a room for me to be good at anything they didn’t approve of.”

There was no self-pity in the words. Toph hated pity too much to carry it openly. There was anger, old and polished smooth from years of handling.

“So you built one,” I said.

“I built a lot.”

“You did.”

Her shoulder pressed against mine.

Not an accident.

“Don’t get weird,” she said.

“I wasn’t.”

“You were about to.”

“Your ability is ruining my emotional privacy.”

“Your emotional privacy is loud.”

I smiled into my water flask.

Toph’s voice changed. Softer, though she would have denied it under oath.

“You don’t treat me like I’m fragile.”

“No.”

“You also don’t do that thing where people get so scared of treating me like I’m fragile that they refuse to help with anything.”

I turned toward her.

Toph kept her face angled toward the courtyard.

“That sounds exhausting,” I said.

“It is.”

“What do you want me to do?”

“Ask.”

The answer came immediately.

“Just ask?”

“Yeah. If I need an arm because we’re on ice, I’ll say yes. If I don’t, I’ll tell you to get lost.”

“That second part sounds familiar.”

“Good. You’re learning.”

We sat there with our shoulders touching.

I thought about all the ways people tried to turn care into guessing. Guessing what someone wanted. Guessing what help meant. Guessing whether love made permission unnecessary.

Toph, for all her bluntness, seemed to hate guessing more than anyone.

“Can I ask you something?” I said.

“You just did.”

“Toph.”

“Fine.”

“Does it bother you when I’m interested in Aang?”

She did not move.

My pulse betrayed me before my courage could.

“And Katara,” I added.

Toph’s mouth curved.

“There it is.”

“What?”

“The actual question.”

I waited.

She tapped two fingers against the stone between us.

“I’ve known those idiots a long time,” she said. “Aang loves like he’s opening every window in a house. Katara loves like she’s building the house around you and then getting mad when you don’t wear a coat.”

I laughed despite myself.

Toph’s grin softened.

“They’re not things I own.”

“No.”

“And neither are you.”

My breath caught.

Her head turned toward me.

“You thought I didn’t know?”

“I don’t know what you know.”

“I know when you lie. I know when Aang walks into a room and your heartbeat gets stupid. I know when Katara touches your arm and it gets stupider.”

I covered my face.

“And,” she continued mercilessly, “I know it does the same thing when I get close.”

The courtyard became very quiet.

I lowered my hands.

Toph was smiling, but not like she had won.

Not exactly.

“Does that bother you?” I asked.

“No.”

The answer landed with startling force.

“Does it scare you?”

Her smile disappeared.

There was the vulnerable edge she usually buried under jokes.

“A little,” she said.

I did not rush to reassure her.

That would have made it smaller than it was.

“What part?”

“The part where people decide closeness means they get to decide things for me.”

I nodded.

“And the part where I might actually want something enough to be mad if it goes away.”

That one hurt differently.

I set my hand on the stone between us, palm up.

Not touching.

An offer.

Toph was blind. She could not see the gesture.

But the shift of my arm moved through the ground.

Her hand found mine.

She laced our fingers together like it annoyed her.

“You’re still terrible at stance,” she said.

“I assumed this meant class was over.”

“It means I’m giving you thirty seconds.”

“For what?”

“To get sappy in your head.”

I squeezed her hand.

Toph squeezed back.

Thirty seconds became a minute.

Neither of us mentioned it.

When we stood, she attacked without warning.

I stepped sideways instead of freezing.

Her hand missed my shoulder.

Toph’s grin was fierce and bright.

“Again.”

This time, I was ready.

The lesson ended only when my arms started shaking badly enough that even Toph admitted the useful part was over.

She sat beside me on a sun-warmed slab of stone while I tried to recover what dignity remained.

“You know,” I said, “most teachers say things like good effort.”

“Most teachers are cowards.”

“You could try encouragement.”

“I encouraged you not to get flattened.”

“That was a threat.”

“Motivating, though.”

I laughed, then winced when every muscle in my shoulders objected.

Toph’s expression shifted toward concern and immediately disguised itself as annoyance.

“You’re going to be sore.”

“I gathered that.”

“Hot bath. Stretch. Don’t let Sugar Queen heal every ache just because she can. Your body should learn what it did.”

There was a philosophy buried inside the insult, as usual.

I looked across the practice yard. “Was Aang really this bad?”

“Worse.”

Aang, approaching with a basket of lunch, called, “I can hear you!”

“I know!”

He sat on my other side. “She made me punch rocks.”

“You were being evasive.”

“I was twelve.”

“Tiny evasive.”

Aang handed me a bun. “For the record, you did great.”

Toph made a gagging sound.

I took the food. “Thank you.”

“Traitor,” Toph said.

But when we stood, she slowed her stride to mine.

Not enough to acknowledge it.

Enough that I noticed.

The ground had a language. So did Toph. Both required paying attention to what happened underneath the obvious thing.

“Again,” Toph said, and this time I laughed before I moved.
